name: Devanagari
signature: A horizontal head-line (shirorekha) runs across the top; letters hang beneath it like laundry on a line.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent 'a' (क = ka). A vowel mark (mātrā) replaces that vowel (क + ी → की = kī). The virama ् strips the vowel, and the bare consonant joins the next into a conjunct (न + ् + म → न्म). The horizontal top line (shirorekhā) runs across the whole word.
notes: Used by Hindi, Marathi, and Sanskrit in this curriculum. The initial inventory below covers the greeting/self-introduction vocabulary; it grows toward a complete set. Stroke orders are the common handwriting convention, not a standard.

strokeOrder: curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
letters.strokeOrderNote: verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the body into more strokes

strokeOrderSource.citation: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari अ stroke order.svg’, frames 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023
strokeOrderSource.variation: The four buildup frames show four ordered pen-down runs: frame 1 starts at the upper-left and carries the upper curve into the lower bowl without lifting; frame 2 restarts at the middle junction and sweeps right through the shoulder; frame 3 descends the right stem top-to-bottom; frame 4 draws the shirorekhā left-to-right, for three intervening lifts. Thomas Egenes, Learning the Sanskrit Alphabet, p. 12 (Maharishi International University Press, 1990), documents a six-stroke traditional Sanskrit form instead. This learner path follows the four-run modern form and fits its joins and directions to Noto Sans Devanagari.

compositionSource.citation: The Unicode Consortium, The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0, Core Specification, §12.1.3 ‘Combining Marks’, U+093C DEVANAGARI SIGN NUKTA (2025)
compositionSource.variation: The standard identifies U+093C as a true diacritic that extends the basic consonant set by adding a subscript dot. The curriculum models the encoded carrier-plus-mark composition explicitly and inventories the seven carrier combinations present in the current Hindi, Marathi, and Sanskrit corpus. Unicode specifies character composition and placement, not a universal handwriting sequence; the carrier-first instruction is therefore a transparent learner convention rather than a claimed normative pen order. Pronunciation and optional retention of nukta vary by language, loanword, and speaker.
